title: Rust glossary: memory, types, and projects

entries.short: Each value has one owner that controls it.
entries.detail: When the owner leaves scope, the value is dropped. This rule provides safe memory management without a separate garbage collector.
entries.example: fn main() { let name = String::from("Rust"); println!("{name}"); }

entries.short: Transfers a value’s ownership to a new binding.
entries.detail: After a value such as `String` is moved, the old binding can no longer be used. This prevents two owners from freeing the same memory.
entries.example: fn main() { let first = String::from("salam"); let second = first; println!("{second}"); }

entries.short: Simple values can be copied instead of moved when assigned.
entries.detail: Small types such as integers are usually `Copy`; `String` is not. Both bindings remain usable after a copy.
entries.example: fn main() { let a = 7; let b = a; println!("{a} {b}"); }

entries.short: Lets code use a value through a reference without moving it.
entries.detail: Passing `&T` to a function does not transfer ownership. The caller can keep using the value afterward.
entries.example: fn size(text: &String) -> usize { text.len() } fn main() { let s = String::from("Rust"); println!("{} {}", size(&s), s); }

entries.short: `&mut T` allows a borrowed value to be changed.
entries.detail: At one time you may have one mutable reference or many shared references, but not both. This helps prevent data races.
entries.example: fn main() { let mut score = 2; let score_ref = &mut score; *score_ref += 3; println!("{score}"); }

entries.short: Describes how long a reference remains valid.
entries.detail: A lifetime annotation does not extend a value’s life; it states how references relate. The compiler can then ensure a returned reference cannot outlive its input.
entries.example: fn longer<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str { if a.len() > b.len() { a } else { b } } fn main() { println!("{}", longer("Rust", "C")); }

entries.short: Borrows a view into part of a collection.
entries.detail: A slice does not own data; it views existing data using a start and length. This example selects two array elements.
entries.example: fn main() { let nums = [2, 4, 6]; println!("{:?}", &nums[1..]); }

entries.short: Groups related named fields into one value.
entries.detail: Access fields with dot notation. A `mut` binding lets you update mutable fields.
entries.example: #[derive(Debug)] struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 } fn main() { let p = Point { x: 2, y: 3 }; println!("({}, {})", p.x, p.y); }

entries.short: Defines the possible variants of a value under one type.
entries.detail: Variants can carry data. Enums make alternatives such as a network message or state explicit.
entries.example: enum Shade { Blue, Red } fn main() { let color = Shade::Blue; match color { Shade::Blue => println!("blue"), Shade::Red => println!("red") } }

entries.short: Checks cases with patterns and can produce a value.
entries.detail: Rust requires `match` arms to cover every case. `_` catches the remainder; explicit variants are often clearer.
entries.example: fn main() { let n = 2; let label = match n { 1 => "one", 2 => "two", _ => "other" }; println!("{label}"); }

entries.short: Handles one matching case with less syntax.
entries.detail: Useful instead of a full `match` when only one case matters. No extra arm is needed for the nonmatching value.
entries.example: fn main() { let value = Some(8); if let Some(n) = value { println!("{n}"); } }

entries.short: Represents a value that may be present or absent.
entries.detail: `Some(value)` carries a value; `None` means there is none. `Option` represents absence explicitly and safely.
entries.example: fn main() { let maybe = Some(4); println!("{}", maybe.unwrap_or(0)); }

entries.short: Returns either a successful value or an error.
entries.detail: `Ok(value)` carries success and `Err(error)` an error. Callers can handle the error instead of silently ignoring it.
entries.example: fn main() { let result: Result<i32, &str> = Ok(9); println!("{}", result.unwrap_or(0)); }

entries.short: Returns an error early, or unwraps a successful value.
entries.detail: The function must return a compatible `Result` or `Option`. `?` shortens error propagation without hiding the error.
entries.example: use std::num::ParseIntError; fn doubled(s: &str) -> Result<i32, ParseIntError> { Ok(s.parse::<i32>()? * 2) } fn main() { println!("{}", doubled("6").unwrap()); }

entries.short: Supplies a fallback value for an error or absence.
entries.detail: A fixed fallback is useful when the program can continue. Prefer `?` or an explicit `match` when the error should be handled or reported.
entries.example: fn main() { let value: Result<i32, &str> = Err("bad input"); println!("{}", value.unwrap_or(0)); }

entries.short: Returns early on `None` and yields the value inside `Some`.
entries.detail: This form makes chained absence checks concise. The function itself must also return an `Option`.
entries.example: fn first_char(s: &str) -> Option<char> { s.chars().next() } fn main() { println!("{:?}", first_char("Rust")); }

entries.short: Immediately reports an unrecoverable program error.
entries.detail: Use `panic!` for unexpected states where continuing is unsafe. For routine cases such as invalid input, `Result` is usually better.
entries.example: fn main() { std::panic::set_hook(Box::new(|_| {})); let result = std::panic::catch_unwind(|| panic!("stop")); println!("{}", result.is_err()); }

entries.short: Clamps an overflowing result to the type’s numeric limit.
entries.detail: `saturating_add` reaches the maximum value instead of panicking or wrapping on overflow. Use it when that boundary behavior is intended.
entries.example: fn main() { println!("{}", u8::MAX.saturating_add(1)); }

entries.short: Defines behavior that a type promises to provide.
entries.detail: A trait declares required methods; implementing types provide that behavior. Generic code can rely on it through trait bounds.
entries.example: trait Greet { fn say(&self) -> &str; } struct Student; impl Greet for Student { fn say(&self) -> &str { "hello" } } fn main() { println!("{}", Student.say()); }

entries.short: Defines methods or trait behavior for a type.
entries.detail: A plain `impl` block adds inherent methods; `impl Trait for Type` implements a trait. A reference receiver makes method calls ergonomic.
entries.example: struct Counter { value: i32 } impl Counter { fn value(&self) -> i32 { self.value } } fn main() { println!("{}", Counter { value: 3 }.value()); }

entries.short: Lets a function work with more than one concrete type.
entries.detail: `<T>` is a type parameter. The compiler often infers `T` from the argument, so one implementation serves multiple types.
entries.example: fn identity<T>(value: T) -> T { value } fn main() { println!("{}", identity(12)); }

entries.short: States which behavior a generic type must provide.
entries.detail: With `T: Display`, a function can format a `T` value. Bounds document which operations generic code may rely on.
entries.example: use std::fmt::Display; fn show<T: Display>(value: T) { println!("{value}"); } fn main() { show(5); }

entries.short: Generates common trait implementations automatically.
entries.detail: `Debug` enables `{:?}` formatting. `derive` removes boilerplate for suitable traits; implement one manually when you need custom behavior.
entries.example: #[derive(Debug)] struct Badge { level: u8 } fn main() { println!("{:?}", Badge { level: 2 }); }

entries.short: An anonymous function that can be stored and may capture values.
entries.detail: Closures use `|parameter| expression` syntax. They can be passed to iterator methods such as `map`, even without capturing values.
entries.example: fn main() { let twice = |n| n * 2; println!("{}", twice(4)); }

entries.short: A sequence that yields elements one at a time.
entries.detail: Iterators are often lazy: they do no work until consumed by methods such as `next` or `sum`. This can avoid unnecessary intermediate collections.
entries.example: fn main() { let total: i32 = [1, 2, 3].iter().sum(); println!("{total}"); }

entries.short: Transforms elements or keeps only those that match a condition.
entries.detail: `map` applies a function to each item; `filter` keeps matching items. The result remains an iterator until consumed.
entries.example: fn main() { let total: i32 = [1, 2, 3, 4].iter().filter(|n| **n > 2).map(|n| n * 2).sum(); println!("{total}"); }

entries.short: Collects iterator items into a collection.
entries.detail: Annotate the result as `Vec<T>` when its type is ambiguous. `collect` consumes the iterator and builds a new collection.
entries.example: fn main() { let squares: Vec<i32> = (1..=3).map(|n| n * n).collect(); println!("{:?}", squares); }

entries.short: Stores same-typed items in a growable sequence.
entries.detail: Stores items in order; indexing out of bounds can panic. Use `get` for an `Option` when an index may be absent.
entries.example: fn main() { let mut nums = vec![1, 2]; nums.push(3); println!("{:?}", nums); }

entries.short: Associates keys with values.
entries.detail: Keys are unique and `insert` replaces an existing value. `get` returns `Option<&V>`, so a missing key is explicit.
entries.example: use std::collections::HashMap; fn main() { let mut scores = HashMap::new(); scores.insert("Ada", 10); println!("{}", scores["Ada"]); }

entries.short: `String` owns text, while `str` is usually viewed through a borrow.
entries.detail: `String` can grow and change; `&str` is a borrowed view. Functions often accept `&str` to work with both literals and `String` values.
entries.example: fn main() { let owned = String::from("hello"); let view: &str = &owned; println!("{view}"); }

entries.short: Groups related code in a namespace.
entries.detail: `mod` declares a module and `pub` exposes an item. Modules organize names and responsibilities as a project grows.
entries.example: mod math { pub fn double(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 2 } } fn main() { println!("{}", math::double(4)); }

entries.short: Controls which names are accessible outside a module.
entries.detail: Items are private to their module by default. Exposing only needed functions keeps an API small and clear.
entries.example: mod api { pub fn version() -> u8 { 1 } } fn main() { println!("{}", api::version()); }

entries.short: Checks a small function or module behavior in isolation.
entries.detail: Tests are commonly written as `#[test]` functions and run with Cargo. This small example executes an assertion and reports success.
entries.example: fn main() { assert_eq!(2 + 2, 4); println!("test passed"); }

entries.short: Creates, builds, and tests Rust projects.
entries.detail: Cargo coordinates the compiler and dependencies. `cargo new`, `cargo build`, `cargo run`, and `cargo test` are common commands.
entries.example: fn main() { println!("Rust project ready"); }

entries.short: Stores a package’s name, version, and dependencies.
entries.detail: The Cargo manifest describes a package. Dependencies go under `[dependencies]`; `Cargo.lock` can record the resolved versions.
entries.example: fn main() { println!("package manifest"); }

entries.short: Finds and runs a project’s tests.
entries.detail: `cargo test` runs unit and integration tests. An assertion failure makes the test process fail as well.
entries.example: fn main() { assert_eq!("rust".len(), 4); println!("checks passed"); }

entries.short: Checks a package’s public behavior as an outside user sees it.
entries.detail: Cargo keeps integration tests in `tests/` and builds each file as a separate test crate. Testing the public API avoids coupling to internals.
entries.example: fn main() { let public_value = 3; assert_eq!(public_value, 3); println!("public API checked"); }

entries.short: Runs work concurrently with the main program.
entries.detail: `std::thread::spawn` starts a thread. `join` waits for its result and reports a panic from that thread.
entries.example: fn main() { let handle = std::thread::spawn(|| 2 + 3); println!("{}", handle.join().unwrap()); }

entries.short: A handle used to wait for a spawned thread.
entries.detail: `join()` returns the thread’s value inside a `Result`. A thread can run without keeping its handle, but the process may finish when the main thread exits.
entries.example: fn main() { let handle = std::thread::spawn(|| "done"); println!("{}", handle.join().unwrap()); }

entries.short: Provides reference-counted shared ownership across threads.
entries.detail: `Arc` uses an atomic reference count and can be shared between threads. Pair it with `Mutex` when shared data must change.
entries.example: use std::sync::Arc; fn main() { let value = Arc::new(7); let other = Arc::clone(&value); println!("{} {}", value, other); }

entries.short: Provides exclusive, synchronized access to shared data.
entries.detail: Locking gives access through a guard. The lock is released automatically when the guard leaves scope.
entries.example: use std::sync::Mutex; fn main() { let count = Mutex::new(1); *count.lock().unwrap() += 2; println!("{}", *count.lock().unwrap()); }

entries.short: Sends messages between threads.
entries.detail: `mpsc::channel` supports multiple producers and one consumer. The sender transmits a message and the receiver reads it.
entries.example: fn main() { let (tx, rx) = std::sync::mpsc::channel(); tx.send("hi").unwrap(); println!("{}", rx.recv().unwrap()); }

entries.short: Mark whether a type can safely move between or be shared across threads.
entries.detail: `Send` means a value can move to another thread; `Sync` means references can be shared across threads. Rust often derives these properties automatically.
entries.example: fn main() { fn assert_send<T: Send>() {} assert_send::<i32>(); println!("i32 is Send"); }

entries.short: Represents its eventual result as a future when called.
entries.detail: Calling an async function creates a `Future`; its body does not simply finish at the call. Running it needs an async runtime and `.await`; the standard library has no executor.
entries.example: async fn answer() -> i32 { 42 } fn main() { let _future = answer(); println!("future created"); }
